Consider 'Living in the house alone does not give you that authority.' The confirm-with-attorney-or-title-company sentence is present, so this is not required.

FAQ item 5 opens with a flat 'No.' Clm:7 says a waiver of the article's requirements is void. Item 1 already notes the exception, but consider 'No, not for a sale the disclosure article covers.' so the short answer does not outrun clm:6.

Item 1 ('Do I have to disclose...') opens with 'California's disclosure article applies, with an exception' rather than a plain yes. Consider starting 'Generally yes, for a sale of single-family residential property' so the quote stands alone. Wording must stay within clm:5, clm:6 and clm:7.

Item 3 ('Can the city or county act...') never says yes or no first. Consider opening with 'Possibly: local officials can act where they find conditions the statute lists.' Keep it tied to clm:1 to clm:4.

Item 5 says 'Planning to skip or soften disclosure can cause disputes later'. This is not tied to a ledger claim. It is soft and appears in the brief's risk row, but consider cutting it or keeping it as general caution.

No answer reads as Northern California or Bay Area specific. Acceptable for a short FAQ whose facts are state law, and no local fact is supported, so nothing was added. Leo may want one local touch in the page body instead.

The last answer lists four routes in four short fragments. It is honest and not a pitch, but it reads like a list. If the writer revises for other reasons, consider one plain lead line such as 'It depends on your time, your money and who can sign.' using no new facts.

classic_text:
Q1. Do I have to disclose the condition of a packed or hoarded house when I sell in California?
A1. For a sale of single-family residential property, California's disclosure article applies, with an exception. The disclosures are made on the Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement form, and any waiver of the requirements is void. Go through the form with an agent or attorney before you list.

Q2. Do I have to clean out a house before selling it?
A2. Not always. It depends on your time, your money, who has authority to sell and which route you pick. Clearing it out shows the real condition before you list. A direct sale is the other route, and a direct buyer prices in the condition.

Q3. Can the city or county act on a packed or hoarded house?
A3. State law lists conditions that can make a building substandard, such as junk and debris that are fire, health or safety hazards. Whether a home meets them is for the local authority. The statute does not mention hoarding. Ask the city or county whether any notice is open.

Q4. Who can sell the house if the owner cannot or will not?
A4. Only someone with legal authority to sign. That might be the owner, a trustee, an executor or administrator, or several heirs who agree. Living in the house does not give that authority. Confirm who can sign with an attorney or title company before you plan anything else.

Q5. Can I agree with the buyer to skip disclosure?
A5. No. Under the California statute, any waiver of the disclosure requirements is void as against public policy. Planning to skip or soften disclosure can cause disputes later. Work through the form with an agent or attorney instead.

Q6. What are my realistic options for a packed or hoarded house?
A6. Keep it while you sort out care and decisions. Clear it out, then list it with an agent. Get professional help first on authority, title and tax. Or sell directly if you want to avoid cleanout and showings and accept that the price reflects the condition.
team_final_text:
Q1. Do I have to disclose the condition of a packed or hoarded house when I sell in California?
A1. California's disclosure article applies to a sale of single-family residential property, with an exception. The disclosures are made on the Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement form, and any waiver of the requirements is void. Ask an agent or attorney how to complete it for your house.

Q2. Do I have to clean out a house before selling it?
A2. It depends on your time, your money, who has authority to sell and the route you pick. Clearing out shows the real condition before you list. A direct buyer prices in the condition. A city or county notice could also change your options.

Q3. Can the city or county act on a packed or hoarded house?
A3. It can look at the property. State law lists conditions that can make a building substandard, such as junk and debris that are fire, health or safety hazards. Whether a home meets them is for the local authority. Ask the city or county whether any notice is open.

Q4. Who can sell the house if the owner cannot or will not?
A4. That depends on who holds title and who has legal authority to sign. A sale can stall when the person living in the house is not that person. Confirm it with an attorney or title company before you plan anything else.

Q5. Can I agree with the buyer to skip disclosure?
A5. No, not for a sale the disclosure rules cover. Under California law, any waiver of the requirements is void as against public policy. Talk it through with your attorney before you sign anything.

Q6. What are my realistic options for a packed or hoarded house?
A6. It depends on what you need most. Keep it while the family sorts out care and decisions. Clear it out and list it if you have time and money. Sell directly to skip cleanout and showings, at a price that reflects condition. Confirm authority and title with an attorney or title company, tax with a CPA.
